summary: Provides a framework and a template for writing specifications of services that network elements offer to applications in networks with multiple qualities of service. It gives context, definitions and suggested data formats, then sets out the template that service documents should follow.

eli5.summary: It is a fill-in-the-blanks form that anyone describing a new network service should use, so all the descriptions look alike.

questions: how to write a network service specification
what is the intserv service template
how to write qos service specification
subtitle: A framework and template for specifying network quality-of-service capabilities.

tldr.problem: The Internet needs a standard way for network elements (routers, switches) to describe the quality-of-service capabilities they offer to applications, so that different services can be deployed consistently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides a framework with precise definitions of QoS concepts (service, flow, traffic specification, request specification) and a detailed template that service specification documents should follow. It includes sections for behavior, motivation, data handling requirements, invocation parameters, exported information, policing rules, and ordering and merging operations.
tldr.outcome: Service specifications that follow this template allow protocol designers to create consistent QoS services and enable different network elements to offer compatible services across the Internet.

today: RFC 2216 is an Informational document that provides the framework used by RFC 2205 (RSVP) and other Integrated Services specifications. It has not been obsoleted and remains the standard template for QoS service specifications.

sections.title: Purpose of the Template
sections.content:
RFC 2216 provides a framework and template for specifying services offered by network elements in an internetwork that supports multiple qualities of service. The goal is to enable applications to request specific network performance characteristics, such as guaranteed bandwidth or low delay, rather than accepting the traditional best-effort service offered by the Internet.

Rather than defining specific services itself, this RFC provides a standardized way for service specifications to be written. Service specifications following this template allow both network elements and application protocols to use consistent terminology and concepts, facilitating interoperability.
sections.eli5: This document says: if you want to offer a new type of network service, here is the form you must fill out and here is what you must describe.

sections.title: Key Concepts and Definitions
sections.content:
RFC 2216 begins with a comprehensive set of definitions. Quality of Service (QoS) refers to parameters like achieved bandwidth, packet delay, and loss rates. A Network Element is any router, switch, subnet, or end-node operating system that handles data packets. A Flow is a set of packets covered by a single QoS request. A Service is a named set of QoS control capabilities offered by a single network element.

Two key parameters are the Traffic Specification (TSpec), which describes the traffic pattern being sent, and the Service Request Specification (RSpec), which describes the desired QoS. The service module enters a contract: it promises to deliver the QoS specified in the RSpec as long as traffic remains within the TSpec bounds.
sections.eli5: A service is like a promise: "If your messages follow the traffic limit (TSpec), we promise to deliver them with this quality (RSpec)."

sections.title: Template Components
sections.content:
Service specifications should include several required sections. The End-to-End Behavior section describes what happens when all network elements along a path offer the same service. The Motivation section explains why the service is useful and what applications might use it. The Network Element Data Handling Requirements section specifies what the network element must actually do with packets: what variables it controls, how precisely, and what guarantees it provides.

The Invocation Information section describes the TSpec and RSpec parameters needed to request the service. The Exported Information section lists what the service module tells other parts of the network (such as setup protocols or management tools). The Policing section defines what happens when traffic exceeds the TSpec. The Ordering and Merging section explains how multiple requests for the same flow are combined.
sections.eli5: Every service specification must explain what it does, why it matters, what parameters you give it, what it tells you back, and what happens if things go wrong.

sections.title: Characterization and Composition
sections.content:
An important concept in RFC 2216 is characterization parameters, which are measurements or estimates exported by a service module that allow the end-to-end behavior to be computed or predicted. For example, a service might export available bandwidth and estimated delay, which can be combined to characterize what an application might experience across a network path.

A composition function takes characterization parameters from multiple network elements and computes the overall end-to-end behavior. Because different network elements may support different services or offer different characterization parameters, the RFC includes a validity flag that indicates whether characterization data is actually available at each hop.
sections.eli5: Each router reports what it thinks will happen to your traffic. By combining these reports from all routers on the path, you can predict the total delay and loss you will see.

sections.title: Data Formats and Naming
sections.content:
RFC 2216 establishes a two-level namespace for services and their parameters: <service_number>.<parameter_number>. Service numbers 1 to 254 are allocated in three regions: number 1 is reserved for generic parameters, numbers 2 to 127 are for IETF-defined services, and numbers 128 to 254 are for experimental or private services.

Service specifications must define the abstract data format for each parameter, including its type (enumeration, numerical value, etc.), range, and precision. Specifications should also define a preferred concrete (packet) format so that protocol designers can efficiently encode the data in messages.
sections.eli5: Every service and every parameter gets a number. Using these numbers, different protocols can all talk about the same services and parameters in a compatible way.
